checkpoints: Understand the JWT structure: header, payload, signature
Install Flask-JWT-Extended and configure a secret key
Implement /register and /login routes that issue tokens
Protect routes with @jwt_required()
Return the current user's identity with get_jwt_identity()

content.value: JSON Web Tokens are the standard for stateless authentication in REST APIs. A JWT is a signed string containing user claims — the server never stores session data. On login, verify credentials, then issue a token with create_access_token(identity=user.id). The client stores the token and sends it in the Authorization: Bearer <token> header on every subsequent request. @jwt_required() verifies the signature and rejects invalid or expired tokens. Use get_jwt_identity() to retrieve the user ID inside a protected route. Never store sensitive data in the token payload — it's base64-encoded, not encrypted.

checkpoints: Install Flask-Migrate and initialize the migrations directory
Generate your first migration after creating a model
Apply the migration with flask db upgrade
Add a column to an existing model and generate a new migration

content.value: db.create_all() works for initial setup but ignores existing tables. Flask-Migrate uses Alembic under the hood to track schema changes incrementally. After install, run flask db init once to create a migrations/ folder. Each time you change a model, run flask db migrate -m 'add email column' to auto-generate a migration script, then flask db upgrade to apply it. Review the generated migration before applying — Alembic doesn't detect all changes (like column renames). Keep migration files in version control alongside your code.

checkpoints: Understand why a single app.py file becomes unmanageable
Create a Blueprint for the auth routes
Create a Blueprint for the items routes
Register both blueprints in the application factory function

content.value: As an API grows, a single file becomes impossible to navigate. Blueprints are Flask's module system — each blueprint groups related routes, error handlers, and utilities. Create auth/routes.py with auth_bp = Blueprint('auth', __name__) and define routes on it. In a create_app() factory function, import and register blueprints: app.register_blueprint(auth_bp, url_prefix='/auth'). The factory pattern also makes testing easy — you can create a fresh app instance per test with test-specific configuration. Organize by feature (auth, items, users) not by file type (routes, models, helpers).

checkpoints: Install marshmallow and define a schema for your model
Validate and deserialize an incoming POST body
Serialize a SQLAlchemy model instance to JSON
Return structured validation errors with field-level messages

content.value: Manual validation with if-else blocks doesn't scale. Marshmallow provides declarative schemas that validate, deserialize (input), and serialize (output) data. Define a schema class with typed fields: fields.String(required=True), fields.Email(), fields.Integer(load_default=0). Call schema.load(request.get_json()) to validate and transform input — it raises a ValidationError with field-level error messages if anything fails. Call schema.dump(model_instance) to serialize a SQLAlchemy object to a dictionary for jsonify(). Using the same schema for both input and output enforces consistency.

checkpoints: Understand why secrets must never be hardcoded
Create a .env file and add it to .gitignore
Load environment variables with python-dotenv
Use a config class to separate development and production settings

content.value: Hardcoded secrets (database URLs, JWT secret keys, API keys) are a security risk and a deployment headache. Store them in a .env file that is never committed to version control. python-dotenv reads .env automatically when you call load_dotenv(). Create a Config class in config.py: SECRET_KEY = os.environ.get('SECRET_KEY') and a DevelopmentConfig subclass with DEBUG = True. Pass the config class to create_app(): app.config.from_object(DevelopmentConfig). This pattern makes switching between development, testing, and production configuration trivial.

checkpoints: Accept file uploads with request.files
Validate file type and size before saving
Save files to a local uploads directory
Return the file URL in the API response

content.value: File uploads require multipart/form-data requests. Read the file with request.files['avatar']. Always validate before saving: check the extension against an allowlist and enforce a size limit. Save with file.save(os.path.join(UPLOAD_FOLDER, secure_filename(file.filename))) — secure_filename() prevents directory traversal attacks. Serve uploaded files with a /uploads/<filename> route using send_from_directory(). For production, serve files from a CDN or object storage (like AWS S3) rather than your application server — it's faster and separates concerns.

moduleTitle: Capstone: Notes App API with Auth
checkpoints: Register and login endpoints that issue JWT tokens
Protect all note endpoints with @jwt_required()
Each user can only see and edit their own notes
Notes have title, content, and updated_at fields
Use blueprints for auth and notes routes
Validate all inputs with Marshmallow schemas
Configure the app using a Config class and .env file

content.value: Your capstone is a multi-user notes API that requires authentication. Every note belongs to a user — enforce this in every query with .filter_by(user_id=get_jwt_identity()). Use blueprints to separate auth and notes logic. Validate inputs with Marshmallow. Store configuration in .env. Run flask db upgrade instead of db.create_all(). Test the full user journey: register, login, create a note, edit it, retrieve it, delete it. Try to access another user's note and confirm you get a 403. This is the kind of complete, secure API you'd build professionally.
